chapter.title: Switching the line on for real

cards.body: Who rings the bell at 8:00 tomorrow while you're still on the train? Up to now, every run of your line started because you pressed the button. **Switching it on means the bell rings with nobody on the factory floor.** The line starts, runs and stops while you're still finding a seat, and the only proof is the logbook by the door.
cards.simpler: Who rings the bell at 8:00 tomorrow while you're still on the train? Until now, your line only ran when you pressed the button. **Switching it on means the bell rings with nobody on the factory floor.** The line starts, runs and stops while you're still looking for a seat. The only proof it happened is the logbook by the door.

cards.prompt: Mia's workflow posts the day's meetings to Slack at 8:00 each weekday. She tested it at 16:00 and it posted. Then she went home without touching the switch. What happens at 8:00 tomorrow?

options.text: It posts, because it already worked once.
Nothing. The workflow isn't switched on, so the trigger never rings the bell.
It posts twice: once as a test, once for real.

whyNot.a: That's a test run, not a switched-on line: a test rings once, when you press it.
whyNot.c: That's mixing up the rehearsal and the real show: a test never repeats by itself.

cards.reteach: A test run is you pulling the bell rope once. The trigger only rings the bell by itself after the workflow is switched on. If it's off, the line just waits, however well it worked yesterday.

cards.title: Handing over the bell
cards.body:
So far you have rung the bell yourself. Pressing *Execute workflow* is a test run: it runs once, right now, and shows each station's output on the canvas while you watch.

**Switching the workflow on hands the bell to the trigger.** The switch is at the top of the editor. It's labelled *Active*, and newer versions call it *Publish*. After that, the schedule, the form or the app rings the bell, day or night.

Those runs don't show up on your canvas. They go into the *Executions* list, n8n's logbook: one line per run, green if it finished, red if it jammed.
cards.simpler: Until now you rang the bell yourself. Pressing *Execute workflow* is a test: one run, with each station's result shown on the canvas. **Switching the workflow on hands the bell to the trigger.** The switch is at the top of the editor, called *Active* or, in newer versions, *Publish*. Then the schedule, form or app rings it, day or night. Those runs go to *Executions*, n8n's logbook: one line per run, green if it finished, red if it jammed.

cards.title: Dana and the staplers
cards.body: Dana in office operations built a line: new row in the Supplies sheet, tidy the fields, check for urgent, post to #office-ops in Slack. Before switching it on at 17:40 on Tuesday, she renamed *Google Sheets1* and *Slack* to *New request row* and *Post to #office-ops*. At 9:05 on Wednesday, Executions showed 6 runs: 5 green, 1 red, stopped at *Post to #office-ops*. **Clear names turn a red mark into an address**, so she knew which station had jammed before clicking anything. The culprit was her manager, asking for more staplers, with the name field left blank.
cards.simpler: Dana in office operations built a line: new Supplies sheet row, tidy, check for urgent, post to #office-ops in Slack. Before switching on at 17:40 Tuesday, she renamed *Google Sheets1* and *Slack* to *New request row* and *Post to #office-ops*. At 9:05 Wednesday, Executions showed 5 green runs and 1 red, stuck at *Post to #office-ops*. **Clear names turn a red mark into an address.** She knew where it jammed before clicking. Cause: her manager wanting staplers, name field blank.

cards.prompt: Leo switched his workflow on at 18:00 last night. It's 9:00 now and he has his coffee. What's the right first check?

options.text: Open the canvas and press Execute workflow to see if it still works.
Open the Executions list and read last night's runs: how many, and green or red.
Wait an hour. If nobody complains, it worked.

whyNot.a: That's a new test run, not a check: it shows the line can work now, not that it did overnight.
whyNot.c: That's using colleagues as the alarm instead of the logbook: silence can also mean the bell never rang.

cards.reteach: Once a workflow is on, the canvas only shows runs you start yourself. Everything the trigger did by itself is written in the Executions list. Read the logbook instead of re-running the machine.

cards.title: Silence is not a green light
cards.body:
You'd think an empty Executions list means a quiet, happy night. Often it means **the bell never rang at all**. A workflow left switched off, a schedule set to the wrong time, or a trigger watching the wrong sheet all leave the same thing behind: nothing.

Where n8n runs matters too. If it runs on your own laptop, the line only works while the laptop is awake. Lid closed at 8:00 means no run, and no red mark to warn you. n8n Cloud or a server stays on.

So the morning check asks two questions: did it run, and did it finish?
cards.simpler: An empty Executions list looks like a quiet night. Often it means **the bell never rang at all**. A workflow left off, a schedule at the wrong time, or a trigger watching the wrong sheet all leave nothing behind. On your own laptop, n8n only works while the laptop is awake. Lid closed at 8:00 means no run and no red mark. n8n Cloud or a server stays on. Each morning, ask: did it run, and did it finish?

cards.body: Sam built a Form Trigger for holiday requests. On Friday they copied the link from the *Test URL* tab, sent it to 9 colleagues and switched the workflow on. Monday's Executions list was empty, because the test link only listens while you're in the editor waiting for a test. Spot it by the address: **a link with *test* in it is the rehearsal bell**, so share the *Production URL* instead.
cards.simpler: Sam built a Form Trigger for holiday requests. On Friday they copied the link from the *Test URL* tab, sent it to 9 colleagues and switched the workflow on. By Monday, Executions was empty. The test link only listens while you sit in the editor waiting for a test. Check the address: **a link with *test* in it is the rehearsal bell**. Share the *Production URL* instead.

cards.prompt: A teammate asks: "Is your Slack summary workflow really live?" Which answer proves it?

options.text: Yes, I pressed Execute workflow and every node went green.
Yes, it's switched on, and the Executions list shows this morning's 8:00 run, finished.
Yes, nobody has reported a problem since I turned it on.

whyNot.a: That's a test run, not a live one: you rang the bell yourself.
whyNot.c: That's silence, not proof: an empty logbook can mean the bell never rang.

cards.reteach: Being live takes two things: the switch is on, and runs appear that you didn't start. Only the Executions list shows the second one. A green canvas or a quiet inbox shows neither.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
Testing is you ringing the bell. Switching on hands the bell to the trigger, so the line runs while you're somewhere else. From then on, the proof is in the Executions list, and **an empty logbook is a question, not a good sign**.

Next: your second line, quicker to build because your app connections are already saved.
cards.simpler: Testing is you ringing the bell. Switching on hands the bell to the trigger, so the line runs while you're somewhere else. After that, the proof lives in the Executions list, and **an empty logbook is a question, not a good sign**. Next up: your second line. It will go faster, because your app connections are already saved.

cards.body: Rename every node in your workflow to a verb plus a thing, like *Post to #team*. Switch it on. Set a phone alarm for 9:00 tomorrow that says: open Executions.
cards.simpler: Rename every node in your workflow, the boxes that act as stations on your line. Give each one **an action word plus a thing**, like *Post to #team*. Then switch the workflow on. Finally, set a phone alarm for 9:00 tomorrow with the label: open Executions.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now switch a workflow on and check the next morning whether it really ran.
